items.prompt: Why does the top layer of your skin never wear down to nothing, even though it flakes away constantly?

options.label: The flakes that fall off settle back onto the skin
options.feedback: Flakes that come off are gone for good; the surface is renewed by cells rising from beneath, not by anything falling back onto it.

options.label: Cells deeper in the skin keep dividing and pushing older cells upward to replace it
options.feedback: Correct — a constant supply of new cells from below replaces what is lost at the surface.

options.label: The skin absorbs material from clothing to rebuild itself
options.feedback: Skin builds its own replacement cells from within the body; it does not draw material from clothing.

options.label: The outer layer stops shedding once it reaches a certain thickness
options.feedback: Shedding never really stops; what keeps the layer from thinning is new cells continually arriving from below to replace what is lost.

items.ok_line: A conveyor belt of new cells rising to replace the old.
items.ko_line: Ask where a replacement cell would have to come from.
items.exp_text: Deep in the skin, a layer of cells divides continually, and each new cell pushes the ones above it a little further toward the surface. As those cells travel upward they flatten, lose their nucleus and fill with a tough protein, until they finally reach the very top as the dead, flat cells that flake away. Because new cells are always being made underneath to take the place of whatever is lost at the top, the skin never runs out even though it is shedding without pause.

items.prompt: Why does a broken bone need to be held still while it heals?

options.label: Stillness stops the bone from growing back the wrong shape
options.feedback: A bone's shape is guided by the cells rebuilding it and by the bone's own structure, not primarily by whether it is held still.

options.label: Movement dries out the bone's blood supply
options.feedback: Movement does not dry out blood vessels; the concern with a healing bone is disrupting the fragile new tissue, not drying anything.

options.label: Movement can break apart the delicate new tissue bridging the broken ends
options.feedback: Correct — that fragile bridge needs stillness to knit properly before it can bear any strain.

options.label: Stillness keeps the surrounding muscles from wasting away
options.feedback: Muscles can weaken during a long period of stillness, but that is a side effect, not the reason a broken bone is held still in the first place.

items.ok_line: A fragile bridge, easily broken again before it has set.
items.ko_line: Think about what movement would do to tissue that has not finished forming yet.
items.exp_text: In the days after a break, the body forms a soft bridge of new tissue across the gap between the broken ends, joining them together before any hard bone has been laid down. That early bridge is far weaker than solid bone and can be torn apart by the same kind of movement or strain that solid bone would shrug off easily. Holding the bone still gives that bridge time to be gradually replaced by tougher tissue and then by new bone itself, layer by layer, without being disturbed while it is still forming.

items.prompt: Why can a small cut to the liver heal and largely restore its original size, while a deep cut to a muscle usually leaves permanent scar tissue instead?

options.label: Liver cells can still divide readily, while many muscle cells lose that ability once mature
options.feedback: Correct — the liver's cells keep the capacity to multiply that most mature muscle cells have largely lost.

options.label: The liver has no blood supply, so nothing there can scar
options.feedback: The liver actually has a very rich blood supply; that is not what explains the difference in how it heals.

options.label: Muscle is simply too far from the heart to receive repair cells
options.feedback: Distance from the heart is not the obstacle; well-supplied muscle still tends to scar because of the type of cells it is built from, not because repair cells cannot reach it.

options.label: The liver feels no pain, so it heals without resistance
options.feedback: Whether an organ senses pain has no bearing on whether its cells can multiply and rebuild lost tissue.

items.ok_line: One tissue can still multiply its own cells; the other mostly cannot.
items.ko_line: Ask what each tissue's own cells are still capable of doing.
items.exp_text: Rebuilding tissue exactly as it was requires living cells of that same type to divide and fill the gap, rather than relying on a patch of generic repair fibres. Liver cells retain a strong capacity to divide throughout life, so after a small injury the surviving cells multiply and gradually regrow tissue very much like what was lost. Mature muscle cells, by contrast, tend to lose that ability to divide once fully formed, so a deep injury there is filled in instead with dense repair fibres that hold the area together but never turn back into working muscle.

items.prompt: Why does a torn fingernail grow back rather than leaving a permanent gap?

options.label: The torn piece slowly repairs its own damaged cells
options.feedback: The visible nail is made of cells that are already dead and hardened; a tear there cannot be repaired, only replaced by new growth from the base.

options.label: Skin around the nail seals over and hardens into new nail
options.feedback: Skin around the nail heals as skin; the nail itself is built only by the dedicated growth centre hidden beneath the base.

options.label: The nail bed pushes the torn piece back into place
options.feedback: A torn nail is not repositioned; it is gradually replaced from the base as new nail material forms and pushes the old nail forward.

options.label: A hidden layer of dividing cells at the nail's base keeps producing new nail
options.feedback: Correct — that hidden growth centre keeps supplying new nail material long after the visible tear.

items.ok_line: The visible nail is already dead; the growing part is hidden underneath.
items.ko_line: Think about where new nail material would actually have to come from.
items.exp_text: The hard, visible nail is made of cells that are already dead and packed with tough protein, which is why cutting or tearing it causes no pain and it cannot repair itself directly. Underneath the skin at the base of the nail sits a hidden patch of living cells that divides constantly, producing new nail material that hardens and is pushed forward beneath the older nail above it. As long as that hidden growth centre is undamaged, it keeps supplying new nail to replace whatever has been torn or worn away at the visible end.

items.prompt: Why does a paper cut on a finger heal faster than a similar-sized cut on the sole of the foot might feel, once it is walked on right away?

options.label: The sole of the foot has no blood vessels to supply repair cells
options.feedback: The sole is well supplied with blood vessels; the slower healing under strain comes from repeated disturbance, not a lack of blood supply.

options.label: Skin on the sole cannot form new cells at all
options.feedback: Skin on the sole forms new cells just as skin elsewhere does; what changes is how much strain that new tissue is put through while it is still fragile.

options.label: Constant pressure and movement can reopen fragile new tissue before it has time to strengthen
options.feedback: Correct — repeated strain on a spot that is still healing keeps disturbing the fragile new tissue there.

options.label: Walking pushes dirt permanently into the wound
options.feedback: Dirt getting into a wound can cause its own problems, but the main reason healing is slowed by immediate walking is the repeated physical strain, not permanent contamination.

items.ok_line: New tissue needs a chance to strengthen before it takes weight again.
items.ko_line: Think about what repeated pressure does to tissue that has only just begun to knit together.
items.exp_text: In the early stages of healing, the tissue bridging a wound is thin and only loosely connected, gaining strength gradually as new fibres are laid down and woven together over time. A cut on a finger used gently can rest while that tissue forms, but a cut on the sole is pressed and stretched with every step, repeatedly disturbing the same fragile bridge before it has had a chance to firm up. That repeated disruption is what can make a wound in a spot under constant load take longer to close than one of the same size somewhere it can rest.

items.prompt: Why does a child's broken bone often heal faster and straighter than the same kind of break in an older adult?

options.label: Bone-building cells are more active in a younger body still growing
options.feedback: Correct — a body still building bone for growth also rebuilds it faster after an injury.

options.label: Children's bones contain no marrow to get in the way of healing
options.feedback: Children's bones do contain marrow, just as adult bones do; it plays no part in slowing or speeding a break's repair.

options.label: Children feel less pain, so they move the healing bone less
options.feedback: Feeling less pain would not by itself make bone tissue form any faster; the difference comes from how active the bone-building cells themselves are.

options.label: A child's bones are made of a completely different material
options.feedback: A child's bones are built from the same kind of material as an adult's; the difference is how actively that material is being produced and replaced.

items.ok_line: A body already busy building bone rebuilds it faster too.
items.ko_line: Ask what a younger, still-growing body is already doing with its bone-building cells.
items.exp_title: A body already primed to build bone
items.exp_text: In a child, the same cells responsible for laying down new bone tissue after an injury are already hard at work every day, lengthening and reshaping bones as the body grows. Because those cells are already so active, they respond to a break by producing new bone tissue quickly, bridging the gap and reshaping it into a smooth, straight bone within a much shorter time. In an older body, bone-building activity has slowed to a slower maintenance pace, so the same repair proceeds far more gradually.

items.prompt: Why does the stomach lining need to constantly repair itself, given how strong its own acid is?

options.label: The acid changes strength throughout the day, giving the lining time to rest
options.feedback: The lining faces some acid exposure at essentially all times; what protects it is constant replacement of its cells, not a pause in the acid itself.

options.label: The acid gradually damages the lining's own cells, which are steadily replaced from below
options.feedback: Correct — the lining renews itself continuously to stay ahead of the damage the acid causes.

options.label: The lining is coated in a material the acid cannot touch at all
options.feedback: The protective mucus coating reduces contact with the acid, but some of the lining's own cells are still affected over time and need ongoing renewal.

options.label: The stomach produces the acid in a separate location, away from the lining
options.feedback: The acid is produced by glands within the lining itself, right where it is needed, not somewhere separate from it.

items.ok_line: Cells worn down by the acid, replaced before the wear becomes a problem.
items.ko_line: Think about what happens to the lining's own cells over time, not just how it is coated.
items.exp_text: The stomach's acid is strong enough that even the mucus layer protecting the lining does not shield it perfectly, and some of the surface cells are worn away or damaged as digestion continues. To keep up, cells deeper in the lining divide rapidly and constantly, moving upward to replace the surface cells almost as fast as they are lost. That steady turnover is what lets the lining keep facing its own acid every day without breaking down.

items.prompt: Why does the lining inside your mouth, such as the inside of a cheek, heal from a bite far faster than skin on your arm heals from a similar cut?

options.label: Saliva seals the wound shut instantly on contact
options.feedback: Saliva offers some chemical protection but does not seal a wound shut by itself; the faster healing comes from how quickly the lining's own cells replace themselves.

options.label: The inside of the cheek has no nerve endings to slow healing down
options.feedback: That lining is full of nerve endings, which is why a bitten cheek is so noticeably painful; nerves are not what determines healing speed here.

options.label: Chewing constantly rubs the wound closed
options.feedback: Chewing puts strain on a wound rather than closing it; the faster healing comes from how quickly new lining cells are produced, not from rubbing.

options.label: Cells in that moist lining divide and replace themselves especially quickly
options.feedback: Correct — the lining inside the mouth renews itself at a notably faster pace than skin does.

items.ok_line: A lining built to renew itself faster than skin ever does.
items.ko_line: Ask what pace the cells of that particular lining normally divide at.
items.exp_title: A lining built for rapid turnover
items.exp_text: The lining inside the cheek is constantly exposed to the wear of chewing, hot food and the general activity of the mouth, so its cells are built to divide and replace themselves at a notably faster pace than the skin on the outside of the body. When that lining is bitten, the same rapid replacement that keeps it renewed under normal wear kicks in to close the wound, bringing new cells across the gap sooner than slower-growing skin could manage. A moist environment also helps by keeping the healing tissue from drying out while it works.

items.prompt: Why does a bruise change colour over the days after it happens, moving from dark red-purple toward yellow-green before fading completely?

options.label: New blood of a different colour keeps replacing the old at the site
options.feedback: No fresh blood is being added to replace what leaked out; the colour change comes from the body slowly breaking down and clearing the blood already trapped there.

options.label: Sunlight reacts with the skin above the bruise to change its shade
options.feedback: The colour changes progress the same way even on skin kept fully covered, since the process happens beneath the surface rather than being driven by light.

options.label: The body gradually breaks down the leaked blood and clears away its coloured components
options.feedback: Correct — each colour reflects a different stage in the breakdown of the same trapped blood.

options.label: The skin cells above the bruise change colour to match it
options.feedback: The skin itself is not changing colour; the shifting shades come from blood trapped underneath being broken down in stages.

items.ok_line: Each shade marks a different stage of the same clean-up.
items.ko_line: Think about what is trapped beneath the skin and what happens to it over time.
items.exp_title: The stages of clearing trapped blood
items.exp_text: A bruise forms when blood leaks out of damaged vessels under the skin and pools in the surrounding tissue, and that pooled blood is what gives a fresh bruise its dark red-purple colour. Over the following days, cells in the area gradually break down the components of that trapped blood, and each of the different substances produced along the way happens to have its own colour, shifting the bruise through blue, green and yellow in turn. Once all of that trapped material has been broken down and carried away, the skin above returns to its normal colour.

items.prompt: Why does hair that has been cut keep growing back from the same spot, over and over, for years?

options.label: A follicle of living, dividing cells beneath the skin keeps producing new hair
options.feedback: Correct — the visible hair is dead, but the follicle producing it underneath keeps working.

options.label: The cut hair itself heals and continues growing from where it was cut
options.feedback: The visible strand of hair is made of dead cells and cannot heal or keep growing; new length comes from the living follicle beneath the skin, not from the cut end regrowing.

options.label: Cutting hair signals nearby skin cells to turn into hair
options.feedback: Skin cells elsewhere do not convert into hair after a cut; growth continues from the same dedicated follicle that was already producing that hair.

options.label: The follicle only produces hair once, and it grows to a fixed length forever
options.feedback: A follicle keeps producing hair over an extended period rather than making just one length and stopping; that is exactly why cut hair keeps coming back.

items.ok_line: The visible hair is dead; the factory beneath it keeps running.
items.ko_line: Ask where a hair actually comes from, beneath the surface you can see.
items.exp_text: The strand of hair you see and cut is made of dead cells packed with tough protein, no different in that respect from the outer layer of skin, which is why cutting it causes no pain and nothing there can regrow on its own. Beneath the skin, though, a small follicle of living cells keeps dividing at the base of that hair, pushing new cells upward to lengthen the strand from below. Cutting the hair simply removes length that has already been produced and pushed out; the follicle underneath is untouched and keeps producing more exactly as it did before.
